title: Kodak Invented the Digital Camera. Then It Lost to It
description:
Kodak built a digital camera in 1975, when engineer Steven Sasson made a prototype that took 23 seconds to save one black-and-white photo. It never went into production, and film kept paying the bills: Kodak's sales were almost $16 billion in 1996. Kodak did go digital and was America's No. 1 digital camera seller in 2005, but its gross margin fell from about 48% (1996) to 15% (2011). Kodak filed for Chapter 11 on January 19, 2012, and weeks later said it would stop making digital cameras. It emerged from bankruptcy in September 2013 as a smaller company focused on printing and imaging for business. The lesson: don't let today's profits decide whether you build tomorrow's business.

Company-wide figures; 1996 includes businesses Kodak later sold (e.g. the Health Group, 2007).

Sources: IEEE Spectrum, 'The First Digital Camera' (Apr 6, 2022); Eastman Kodak Form 10-K for 1996 (sales $15,968M, cost of goods sold $8,326M; gross margin computed); Associated Press via NBC News (Feb 9, 2006), citing IDC (24.9% US share in 2005); Eastman Kodak Form 10-K for 2011 (sales $6,022M, gross profit margin 15%, Chapter 11 filing and Feb 9, 2012 phase-out of digital cameras); Kodak 8-K (Sept 3, 2013) on emerging from Chapter 11. Educational content, not investment advice.

scenes.say: In nineteen seventy-five, Kodak built a digital camera. Why did Kodak lose?
Steve Sasson's prototype took twenty-three seconds to save one photo.
It never went into production. Film still paid the bills.
By nineteen ninety-six, sales hit almost sixteen billion dollars.
Now the twist: Kodak did go digital.
By two thousand five, it was America's top digital camera seller.
The catch: Kodak's gross margin fell from forty-eight percent to fifteen.
In January twenty twelve, Kodak filed for bankruptcy.
Weeks later, it announced an exit from digital cameras.
The lesson: protect tomorrow's business, not just today's profits.
Inventing the future isn't enough. Ask Kodak.
